title: What Cronbach's Alpha Is and What Counts as Acceptable
meta_title: Cronbach's Alpha: what it measures, what passes | DoThesis
meta_description: What Cronbach's alpha measures, where the 0.6 and 0.7 thresholds come from, how to read Item-Total Statistics in SPSS, and what to do when the coefficient is low.
excerpt: Cronbach's alpha measures scale reliability: what the number means, which threshold applies to your scale, and how to act on a low one.
body:
You run Reliability Analysis for the first time, SPSS returns a Cronbach's alpha of 0.612, and you have no idea what that number says about your scale. Keep the items, or drop one, and if you drop one, which one.

This article answers those three questions in the order you will need them with the data file open: what the coefficient measures, what a committee accepts, and what to do when the number comes back low.

## What Cronbach's alpha measures

Cronbach's alpha is a coefficient of internal consistency reliability for a set of items meant to measure one construct (Cronbach, 1951). In plain terms, it asks whether the items in one scale are talking about the same thing.

The coefficient is computed from the number of items in the scale and the average correlation between them. More items, and items that correlate more strongly with each other, push alpha up. Values run from 0 to 1, and in practice you will meet a negative one the first time a reverse-coded item is left un-reversed.

Hold on to one distinction from the start. Alpha speaks about reliability, not about validity. A scale can be perfectly consistent and still measure a construct you did not intend to measure. Reliability is the necessary condition, and convergent and discriminant validity are the rest of the story (Fornell and Larcker, 1981).

There is a second distinction worth having early. Alpha is a property of a set of items in one sample, not a property of the instrument in the abstract. The same questionnaire can return 0.88 in the study you borrowed it from and 0.61 in yours, and the difference usually lives in the translation, the response scale or the respondents rather than in the items.

## Why reliability comes first in a quantitative thesis

In a quantitative thesis, alpha is the first gate every scale passes through. You run it before exploratory factor analysis, and only the items that survive go into the factor solution.

The reason is practical. If a scale is not consistent, every number downstream carries that noise: loadings drift, regression coefficients shrink, and a hypothesis gets rejected because of measurement rather than because the relationship is absent.

This is also the part a committee questions most often, because it is the easiest part to check. A complete reliability table with corrected item-total correlations and the alpha-if-item-deleted column shows that you ran the analysis rather than copying a scale out of a published paper.

Run it construct by construct, never on the whole questionnaire at once. A single alpha computed over forty items from six different constructs is a number with no meaning, and it is one of the two mistakes that reliably come up at a defence. The other one is further down this page.

## What counts as an acceptable alpha

The threshold depends on whether the scale is established or you are building a new one. The table below collects the cut-offs quoted most often in theses, with the source you can cite for each.

| Value | Reading | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alpha at 0.7 or above | The scale is reliable, the standard bar for an established instrument | (Nunnally, 1978) |
| Alpha from 0.6 to below 0.7 | Acceptable for a new construct or exploratory research | (Hair et al., 2010) |
| Alpha from 0.8 to 0.9 | A good scale, the usual range for original marketing instruments | (Hair et al., 2010) |
| Alpha above 0.95 | Suspect redundant items, consider shortening the scale | (Hair et al., 2010) |
| Corrected item-total correlation at 0.3 or above | The condition for keeping an item in the scale | (Nunnally and Bernstein, 1994) |

Two things the table does not say.

First, alpha rises with the number of items. An eight-item scale clears 0.8 easily even when the items correlate only moderately, so a high alpha on a long scale is weak evidence about the scale itself.

Second, the 0.6 floor belongs to research that is genuinely exploratory. Using it for a scale you borrowed unchanged from a published study is the version of this rule a committee notices, and the follow-up question is what happened to the instrument on the way into your sample.

The upper bound surprises people. An alpha of 0.97 is not a better result than 0.85, it is a sign that several items are asking the same question in different words, and a shorter scale would carry the same information with less respondent fatigue.

## Reading the reliability output

Open `Analyze > Scale > Reliability Analysis`, move the items of one construct into the Items box, open the `Statistics` button and tick `Scale if item deleted`. SPSS prints Reliability Statistics first and Item-Total Statistics underneath it.

The table below is illustrative output for a five-item satisfaction scale, not results from a real dataset. Read the last two columns together.

| Item | Corrected item-total correlation | Cronbach's alpha if item deleted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SAT1 | 0.641 | 0.802 |
| SAT2 | 0.588 | 0.815 |
| SAT3 | 0.702 | 0.787 |
| SAT4 | 0.214 | 0.861 |
| SAT5 | 0.615 | 0.808 |

The overall alpha for this scale is 0.834. SAT4 correlates 0.214 with the rest of the scale, below the 0.3 condition, and removing it would raise alpha to 0.861. That item is the candidate for deletion.

Notice what the last column does not tell you. It reports what alpha would become, not whether the construct still covers what it claimed to cover once the item is gone. That judgement is yours, and it belongs in the text of your methodology chapter.

## What to do when alpha is too low

Work in rounds, and write down each round. Reliability analysis rarely comes out clean on the first run, and dropping an item, running again and recording what changed is ordinary practice rather than evidence that you did something wrong.

Check the reverse-coded items first. One item left un-reversed can drag a healthy scale under 0.5 on its own, and recoding it through `Transform > Recode into Different Variables` costs a minute. This is the second mistake that comes up at a defence, and it is the cheaper one to fix.

Drop one item at a time, the one with the lowest corrected item-total correlation, and rerun. Dropping three at once hides which item was the problem, and you will be asked which one it was.

Stop when the scale has three items left. A two-item construct is not a scale, and shrinking a construct to keep a coefficient happy is a measurement decision that a reader will treat as one.

If the scale still fails at three items, the problem is upstream of the analysis. Look at how the items were translated, whether the response scale was labelled at every point, and whether the respondents had any reason to read two of the items as the same question.

## How to write this in your thesis

You can adapt the sentence below. Replace the bracketed parts with your own numbers, and keep the source, because the threshold is the part that needs one.

**Reliability of the [Satisfaction] scale was assessed using Cronbach's alpha. The scale returned an alpha of [0.834], above the 0.7 threshold recommended for established instruments (Nunnally, 1978). One item, [SAT4], was removed because its corrected item-total correlation of [0.214] fell below the 0.3 condition, after which alpha rose to [0.861]. The [4] remaining items were retained for exploratory factor analysis.**

State the number of items you kept, not only the coefficient. A reader who knows that alpha rises with scale length will look for it, and a sentence that reports a coefficient without a count invites the question rather than answering it.

Put the full reliability table in the appendix and the summary in the chapter. A table of six constructs with their item counts and their alphas is what a reader wants in the body of the text.

Read more: [exploratory factor analysis in SPSS](/blog/en/exploratory-factor-analysis-in-spss), [sample size for a thesis survey](/blog/en/sample-size-for-a-thesis-survey), [the SPSS topic hub](/blog/en/chu-de/spss) and [the rest of the English bank](/blog/en).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is an alpha of 0.6 enough for a master's thesis

It can be, for a construct you built yourself or adapted heavily, and Hair et al. (2010) is the source to cite for it. For a scale taken unchanged from a published study, 0.6 invites the question of what went wrong in translation or in the sample, so treat it as a signal rather than as a pass.

### Can I delete items until alpha is high enough

You can delete the items that fail the corrected item-total correlation condition, and you should say that you did. Deleting past that point to chase a number changes what the scale measures, and a three-item construct that started as seven is visible to anyone who reads your appendix.

### Why is my Cronbach's alpha negative

Almost always a reverse-coded item that was never recoded. Check the wording of every item against the direction of the scale, recode the negative ones, and run the analysis again before you look for a deeper explanation.

### Do I still need alpha if I use SmartPLS

You report composite reliability and average variance extracted in a PLS model, and alpha is usually reported beside them as the conservative lower bound (Hair et al., 2019). Reporting all three is normal, and reporting none of them is not.

Once the scales hold, the next step is the factor solution, and the same items go into it. DoThesis runs that stage on your own `.sav` file in module M4, from the reliability table through to the rotated component matrix, so you can see [what the workspace does with your data](/landing) before you decide how to spend the week.
